Slot 6 = LDP's pro-Beijing AA-ken; slot 7 = Mishima's Tatenokai; slot 0 = Kishi/Sasakawa anti-communist federation.

0.name: Kokusai Shōkyō Rengō
0.english: International Federation for Victory over Communism
0.text:
The International Federation for Victory over Communism was founded in 1968 by Sun Myung Moon's Unification Church together with the right-wing financier Sasakawa Ryōichi, its honorary chairman, under the patronage of former Prime Minister Kishi Nobusuke. Chaired by Kuboki Osami, it is part of the anti-communist network around the World Anti-Communist League and mobilises young activists against the student left.

It stands for militant anti-communism, a strengthened alliance with the United States, South Korea and Taiwan, revision of the postwar constitution and a strong state able to crush subversion. Its leverage lies in Sasakawa's motorboat-racing fortune, Kishi's influence over the LDP's right wing and the disciplined cadres of the Unification Church.

1.name: Jiyū-Minshutō
1.text:
The Liberal Democratic Party has governed Japan since its founding in 1955. Prime Minister Satō Eisaku, in office since 1964, has just won a landslide in the general election of 27 December 1969 with 288 seats, after securing President Nixon's pledge to return Okinawa in 1972. The party is a federation of factions led by Satō, Fukuda Takeo, Miki Takeo, Nakasone Yasuhiro and others, with Tanaka Kakuei as Secretary-General.

It stands for high-speed growth, the security treaty with the United States, due for automatic extension this June, and pragmatic relations with Asia. Its base lies in farmers, small business, big industry and the bureaucracy, and its strength in money politics and rural constituencies.

2.name: Minshu Shakaitō
2.text:
The Democratic Socialist Party broke away from the Japan Socialist Party in 1960 under Nishio Suehiro, rejecting its Marxism and its campaign against the security treaty. Led since 1967 by Nishimura Eiichi, it won 31 seats in the December 1969 election and is backed by the moderate Dōmei labour federation of private-sector unions.

It stands for parliamentary democracy, welfare-state reform and anti-communism, accepts the American alliance while seeking a more equal partnership, and favours cooperation between labour and management. Its voters are private-sector unionists, white-collar employees and small entrepreneurs, and it is the most likely partner should the Liberal Democrats ever need one.

3.name: Nihon Shakaitō
3.text:
The Japan Socialist Party is the main opposition, but the December 1969 election was a disaster: it fell from 140 to 90 seats. Chairman Narita Tomomi presides over a party split between Eda Saburō's reformist 'structural reform' wing and the Marxist Socialist Association of Sakisaka Itsurō, which dominates the youth and union cadres.

It upholds unarmed neutrality, opposes the US–Japan Security Treaty and the Self-Defense Forces, defends the pacifist Constitution and calls for recognition of Beijing. Though rhetorically Marxist, it belongs to the Socialist International alongside Western labour parties, and it relies on the public-sector unions of Sōhyō and on urban voters.

4.name: Nihon Kyōsantō
4.text:
The Japanese Communist Party, founded in 1922 and legal since 1945, has been rebuilt under Secretary-General Miyamoto Kenji into a disciplined mass party, with the veteran Nosaka Sanzō as chairman. It broke with Moscow in 1964 and with Beijing in 1966, and in the December 1969 election it nearly tripled its seats to 14 with almost seven per cent of the vote.

It follows an 'independent' line: a parliamentary road to socialism, opposition to the security treaty and American bases, and fierce hostility to the violent New Left it brands as Trotskyists. Its strength lies in its newspaper Akahata, its youth league Minsei and solid support in the cities and among teachers and doctors.

5.name: Zengakuren
5.text:
Zengakuren, the All-Japan Federation of Students' Self-Government Associations, has splintered into rival sects of the New Left: the Chūkaku-ha and Kakumaru-ha of the Revolutionary Communist League, the Bund factions and, since September 1969, the Red Army Faction, many of whose members were arrested at Daibosatsu Pass in November. The campus struggles of 1968–69, culminating in the siege of Tokyo University's Yasuda Auditorium, have been broken by riot police.

The sects preach world revolution against both American imperialism and Soviet Stalinism and prepare for the '1970 struggle' against the security treaty. Their weapons are helmets, staves, Molotov cocktails and street battles, and they draw on students and young workers disillusioned with the Socialists and Communists alike.

6.name: Ajia-Afurika Mondai Kenkyūkai
6.text:
The Afro-Asian Problems Study Group is a caucus of Liberal Democratic Party members formed in 1965 in opposition to the pro-Taiwan Asian Problems Study Group. Led by Utsunomiya Tokuma, Fujiyama Aiichirō and the veteran Matsumura Kenzō, who keeps the memorandum trade with Beijing alive, it is a vocal minority within the ruling party.

Conservative and nationalist but sceptical of American hegemony, it calls for normalising relations with the People's Republic, ending Japan's complicity in the Vietnam War, expanding trade with China and the Soviet bloc and pursuing an independent Asian diplomacy. Its leverage lies in business interest in the China market and in its direct contacts with Zhou Enlai.

7.name: Tatenokai
7.text:
The Tatenokai, the Shield Society, is a private militia of about a hundred students founded in October 1968 by the novelist Mishima Yukio. Its members train with the Ground Self-Defense Force at the foot of Mount Fuji, wear uniforms Mishima designed and swear loyalty to the Emperor; in November 1969 they paraded on the roof of the National Theatre for the society's first anniversary.

It rejects the American-written constitution and the materialism of postwar Japan, and calls for the Emperor to be restored as the sacred centre of the nation and for the Self-Defense Forces to become a true national army. Mishima hopes that unrest over the security treaty will compel the army to act, and the society's leverage lies in his fame and his contacts among officers.

8.name: Perushia-kai
8.text:
The Persia Circle brings together Iranian traders, oil engineers and students in Tokyo and Kobe with Japanese scholars of Persian at the Tokyo University of Foreign Studies, meeting for Nowruz, Muharram commemorations and discussion evenings. Japan's growing dependence on Iranian oil gives it a small but respectable place in business circles.

Its members follow the reformist Shia thought heard in Tehran's lecture halls, seeking to reconcile faith with science, social justice and national development, and they admire the Islamic philosophy that Izutsu Toshihiko is introducing to Japanese readers. Loyal to the Shah's alliance with the West, they hope to make Japan a partner of a modern Muslim Iran.

9.name: Anjoman-e Eslami
9.text:
The Islamic Society of Iranian Students is a clandestine circle of religious Iranian students in Tokyo, linked to the Muslim student associations Iranians abroad are building in Europe and North America. They gather in rented rooms to read the declarations of Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, exiled by the Shah and teaching in Najaf since 1965, and avoid the eyes of SAVAK informers at the embassy.

They brand the Shah a tyrant and an American puppet, denounce Japan's oil deals with his regime and call for an Islamic government led by the clergy. Hostile to Washington and Moscow alike, they have no base in Japanese society and rely on contacts with fellow students abroad.

10.name: Nihon Musurimu Kyōkai
10.text:
The Japan Muslim Association, founded in the early 1950s by Japanese converts who had encountered Islam in wartime China and Southeast Asia, is the main organisation of Japan's few native Muslims. Supported by Saudi Arabia and the Muslim World League, it organises pilgrimages and religious instruction, and its veteran Umar Mita Ryōichi is preparing a Japanese translation of the Koran.

It stands for a quietist Sunni establishment Islam loyal to the Saudi kingdom and to the Japanese state: correct worship, halal provision, education and friendship with the oil-producing monarchies. Its leverage lies in its role as intermediary between Japanese business and the Gulf states on which Japan's industry increasingly depends.

11.name: Halaqat al-Khilafa
11.text:
The Caliphate Study Circle is a handful of Arab, Pakistani and Indonesian students in Tokyo, together with a few Japanese converts, who read the pamphlets of Hizb ut-Tahrir and Sayyid Qutb's 'Milestones' and debate the restoration of the caliphate abolished in 1924. They meet at the Tokyo Mosque and in student hostels, largely ignored by the police.

They regard nation-states, monarchies and Arab socialist regimes alike as betrayals of Islam, call for a single caliphate under the sharia uniting Muslims from Morocco to Indonesia, and approve armed struggle against Israel and its Western patrons. Their leverage is negligible beyond the hostels and the anger stirred among Muslim students by the 1967 war.

12.name: Nihon Musurimu Gakusei Kyōkai
12.text:
The Muslim Students Association of Japan was founded in Tokyo in the early 1960s by young Japanese converts together with Muslim students from Asia and the Arab world. It runs study circles, Arabic classes and summer camps, and its members dream of founding a permanent Islamic centre for Japanese Muslims.

Its outlook mirrors that of the Muslim Brotherhood and of Abul Ala Maududi's Jamaat-e-Islami: Islam as a complete way of life, renewal through education and preaching, social welfare and a moral alternative to postwar materialism. Peaceful and law-abiding, it draws its leverage from links with Muslim student federations abroad and patrons in the Gulf.

13.name: Tsūshō Sangyōshō
13.english: Ministry of International Trade and Industry
13.text:
The Ministry of International Trade and Industry is the pilot agency of Japan's economic miracle, steering industry through administrative guidance, licences, foreign-exchange allocation and loans from the Japan Development Bank. Its minister is Ōhira Masayoshi, but real power lies with an elite of career bureaucrats from Tokyo University's law faculty.

Its creed is developmentalism: target strategic industries, merge firms into national champions such as the new Nippon Steel due to form this spring, shield them from foreign capital while liberalisation is phased in, and conquer export markets. Technocratic and above party, it answers neither to Washington nor to the voters, and its leverage lies in permits, credit and the revolving door into industry.

14.name: Kōmeitō
14.text:
Kōmeitō, the Clean Government Party, was founded in 1964 as the political arm of the Sōka Gakkai, the lay Buddhist movement of Nichiren Shōshū led by Ikeda Daisaku; its chairman is Takeiri Yoshikatsu. In the December 1969 election it won 47 seats to become the third-largest party, but it is now engulfed in scandal over attempts to suppress Fujiwara Hirotatsu's critical book on the Sōka Gakkai.

It preaches 'humanitarian socialism' and a middle way between capitalism and communism, stressing welfare, clean politics, pacifism and normal relations with China. Neutral between the blocs, it draws its voters from small shopkeepers, housewives and urban migrants mobilised by the Sōka Gakkai's tightly organised membership.

15.name: Keizai Dantai Rengōkai
15.text:
Keidanren, the Federation of Economic Organizations, is the peak body of Japanese big business and the paymaster of the Liberal Democratic Party. Chaired since 1968 by Uemura Kōgorō, successor to Ishizaka Taizō, it groups the steel, electrical, shipbuilding and banking giants and the keiretsu that grew out of the old zaibatsu.

It favours high growth, low taxes on industry, cautious liberalisation of trade and capital, cooperative labour relations and the American alliance, while lobbying for markets and resources in Southeast Asia. Its leverage lies in channelling political donations to the LDP's factions and in the close personal ties between its leaders, ministers and senior bureaucrats.

16.name: Keizai Dōyūkai
16.text:
The Japan Association of Corporate Executives, Keizai Dōyūkai, was founded in 1946 by young managers who took charge of companies after the purge of the old zaibatsu owners. Led by Kikawada Kazutaka of Tokyo Electric Power, it is the reformist, individual-membership voice of business, distinct from the industry associations of Keidanren.

It advocates free markets, deregulation, liberalisation of trade and foreign investment, fiscal discipline and the social responsibility of managers, and criticises cartels, bureaucratic guidance and protected sectors such as agriculture. Its leverage lies in ideas, policy studies and the personal standing of its executives with ministers and the press.

17.name: Minamata-byō Taisaku Shimin Kaigi
17.english: Citizens' Council for Minamata Disease Countermeasures
17.text:
The Citizens' Council for Minamata Disease Countermeasures was founded in Minamata in January 1968 by local residents, among them the writer Ishimure Michiko, to support the victims of mercury poisoning by the Chisso chemical plant. In September 1968 the government finally acknowledged Chisso's responsibility, and in June 1969 twenty-nine patient families filed suit for damages in Kumamoto.

It belongs to a wave of citizens' movements against pollution, from Yokkaichi asthma to itai-itai disease, that demand compensation, corporate accountability, strict emission limits and the right to a healthy environment over unchecked growth. Its leverage lies in the courtroom, the newspapers and the moral authority of the victims.

18.name: Nihon Rōdō Kumiai Sōhyōgikai
18.english: General Council of Trade Unions of Japan
18.text:
The General Council of Trade Unions of Japan, Sōhyō, is the country's largest labour federation, with over four million members concentrated in the public sector: railways, post, teachers and local government. Led by Secretary-General Iwai Akira and shaped by Ōta Kaoru, father of the annual 'spring offensive' wage campaign, it is the organisational backbone of the left.

Militant and neutralist, it stands for higher wages, the right to strike for public employees, opposition to the security treaty and American bases, and unarmed neutrality. It supplies the Socialists with money, candidates and votes, and its leverage lies in unions that can bring the railways and schools to a halt.
18.wiki: General Council of Trade Unions of Japan

19.name: Nihon Kyōsantō (Saha)
19.text:
The Japanese Communist Party (Left) was constituted in 1969 by pro-Chinese communists expelled from the JCP after Miyamoto Kenji's break with Beijing in 1966, with its strongest base in the former Yamaguchi prefectural committee. It is small but enjoys the open favour of the Chinese Communist Party, whose press hails it as Japan's genuine revolutionaries.

Maoist and anti-revisionist, it denounces both American imperialism and Soviet revisionism, upholds Mao Zedong Thought and the Cultural Revolution, and calls for a people's democratic revolution to drive out the US bases. Its leverage lies in Beijing's patronage, in friendship-trade firms dealing with China and in pockets of support among workers in western Honshu.

20.name: Nippon Izokukai
20.text:
The Japan Association of War-Bereaved Families represents the relatives of the more than two million servicemen killed in the Pacific War, with chapters in every prefecture. Its president is Kaya Okinori, finance minister in Tōjō's wartime cabinet, convicted as a war criminal and later rehabilitated as a Liberal Democratic politician.

It is the driving force behind the Yasukuni Shrine bill, first submitted to the Diet in 1969, which would place the shrine under state support, and it campaigns for pensions, national honour for the war dead and patriotic education. Its leverage lies in a nationwide network of local chapters that delivers votes to conservative candidates.

21.name: Dai Nippon Aikokutō
21.text:
The Greater Japan Patriotic Party was founded in 1951 by Akao Bin, a prewar ultranationalist who harangues passers-by from sound trucks in Tokyo's Ginza. Its former member Yamaguchi Otoya assassinated Socialist chairman Asanuma Inejirō on live television in 1960, and the party remains a magnet for the street activists of the right.

It preaches emperor worship, anti-communism and violent hostility to the left, demands rearmament and the return of territories held by the Soviet Union, and backs the American alliance as a bulwark against Moscow and Beijing. Its leverage lies in intimidation, street presence and ties to conservative patrons and the underworld.

22.name: Jieitai
22.text:
The Japan Self-Defense Forces, created in 1954 under the civilian Japan Defense Agency, number about a quarter of a million men in ground, maritime and air branches. Many senior officers are veterans of the imperial forces; they operate under the Third Defense Buildup Plan of 1967–71 but remain politically marginal, constitutionally contested and barred from service abroad.

The officer corps quietly favours constitutional revision, a larger defence budget and a more equal partnership with the United States, and resents the hostility of the left, the press and the universities. Its leverage lies in the rising defence budget, in American backing and in the patronage of the LDP's defence hawks.

23.name: Kōshitsu
23.text:
The Imperial House of Japan, the world's oldest hereditary monarchy, is headed by Emperor Hirohito, on the throne since 1926 and reduced by the 1947 Constitution to 'the symbol of the State and of the unity of the people'. Crown Prince Akihito and Crown Princess Michiko embody the popular, modern face of the dynasty, while the Imperial Household Agency guards its rites.

Around the throne gather those who want its status raised again: Shinto priests, veterans and nationalists calling for the Emperor to be named head of state and for official homage at Yasukuni, encouraged by the restoration of National Foundation Day in 1967. The dynasty itself stays aloof from politics, but its prestige is the deepest reservoir of national feeling.
